draft.title: Writing critically
card: Descriptive writing says what a text is about or what happens in it. Critical writing goes further and asks questions about the text or idea.
A critical writer asks whose views the text presents and who benefits from them. They also ask whose views are left out.
A critical writer backs each point with evidence from the text, such as word choices, images or who is quoted.
Example: a council flyer about a new car park lists only the views of shop owners. A critical comment is that it leaves out residents who live nearby.
draft.remember: Critical writing questions a text. It does not just retell it.

a.q: Which sentence is an example of critical writing about an advertisement for a phone?
opts: The ad shows only wealthy buyers, so it ignores other people
The ad shows a woman using a phone on a train
The ad lasts thirty seconds and has upbeat music
The ad begins in a kitchen and ends in a park
a.why: This sentence questions whose people the ad includes and who it leaves out. The other options only describe what appears in the ad, which is not critical writing.
a.clue: Which one asks who is missing, not what is shown?

b.q: Tariq is writing about a news article on a new mine near a town. It quotes the mining company three times and no local farmers. Which sentence from Tariq is the most critical?
opts: The article favours the company by ignoring local farmers
The article quotes the company's spokesperson three times
The article is about a mine that may open near a town
The article has a headline, a photo and four paragraphs
b.why: This sentence judges whose views the article serves and whose it leaves out. The sentence about three quotes is tempting, but it only reports a detail without asking what that detail means.
b.clue: Look for the sentence that explains what the detail means.

a.best: The ad shows only wealthy buyers, so it ignores other people

b.best: The article favours the company by ignoring local farmers

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is clearly the longest and the only one with a 'so' reasoning clause. The clue ('asks who is missing') also points straight to it, since no other option mentions anyone missing. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.
Why (a) says 'questions whose people the ad includes', which is ungrammatical and confusing. It could read 'questions which people the ad includes and who it leaves out'.
